h1:
Trang in 3 Days, 2 Nights
Town + Island Tour + Sleeping on an Island
intro: Three days and two nights is the sweet spot for Trang — enough to see both sides of the province in one trip. Day one stays in town for roast pork and an early dim sum breakfast and a wander through old Kantang. Day two you board a boat to hit the Emerald Cave and Koh Kradan, then skip the trip back to the mainland and sleep on an island for a night, so you wake up to a sea that the crowds haven't reached yet. Day three is an easy morning swim off the beach before the boat home. We've laid out every day with times, prices, real island stays and the spots we last checked in 2026.

blocks.html: This plan is built for people who want both the town and the sea, taken slowly. What sets it apart from a single-day trip is that on the second night you sleep on an island instead of catching the evening boat back to shore. Staying over means you get the sea in the morning before the first tour boats arrive — quiet beach, still water, the stretch a lot of people say is the best part of the whole trip. We've folded the island accommodation and the boat logistics into each day for you.

blocks.title: Read this before you start
blocks.html: This plan assumes the November–April window, when the Trang sea is clear and the boats reliably run. If you come during the August–September monsoon when the seas are rough, some islands close and the Emerald Cave usually shuts — swap day two for a land day instead, such as the Khao Kob sea cave or a waterfall up in the Banthat range.

blocks.text: What This 3-Day Trip Looks Like Overall

blocks.html: Before the day-by-day, here's the big picture of what each day focuses on, in case you want to reorder things to fit your flight or train times.

items.name: Day 1 — Trang town + Kantang
items.blurb: Start the morning with roast pork and dim sum, the dishes Trang is known for, then walk the old streets in the center. In the afternoon, drive out to Kantang to see the old wooden railway station, and end the day watching the sunset at Pak Meng beach before sleeping near the coast to catch the morning boat.

items.name: Day 2 — Island tour + overnight
items.blurb: Board the boat early, swim the Emerald Cave at Koh Mook, snorkel at Koh Cheuak, then get dropped at Koh Kradan or Koh Mook for the night. Come evening, the whole beach is yours once the tour boats have all gone back.

items.name: Day 3 — Beach morning + home
items.blurb: Wake to a quiet sea, swim or paddle a SUP off the beach in the morning, have a relaxed breakfast, then take the boat back to shore. Squeeze in one last Trang meal before you move on.

blocks.text: Day 1 — Walk Trang Town for Roast Pork, Dim Sum and Kantang

blocks.html: No rush on day one — spend it getting to know Trang town first. This town is built on Hokkien-Chinese food, and roast pork with dim sum is a breakfast locals genuinely eat. Kantang, meanwhile, is an old port town with wooden buildings and the end-of-the-line railway station to wander.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Trang town + Kantang + Pak Meng beach

items.activity: Roast pork breakfast at a long-running shop like Trang Moo Yang or Go Sui, with old-school coffee on the side
items.note: Trang roast pork has crisp skin and tender meat, eaten with sweet dipping sauce. The famous shops sell it early and sell out fast — get there before 9 a.m. to be safe.

items.activity: Follow up with hot baskets of dim sum at a place in town like Chen Jia Dim Sum Café, with Chinese tea alongside
items.note: Trang dim sum comes in small baskets, roughly ฿15–25 each. Order several kinds and share.

items.activity: Walk the streets in the center to see the Sino-Portuguese shophouses, stopping at a café like Gray 18 or RumLuk Café for a coffee
items.note: Trang town is easy walking, with everything close by — old coffee shops and old buildings trade off down the lanes.

items.activity: Drive out to Kantang district, about 45 minutes, and have a Southern Thai or roadside seafood lunch
items.note: Kantang sits south of town. It's an old port, quieter than the town center.

items.activity: Walk around Kantang railway station, a colonial yellow-and-red wooden building — the last stop on the Andaman side
items.note: It's a classic Trang photo spot, an old building still in real use, and free to visit.

items.activity: Drive to Pak Meng beach in Sikao district to catch the sunset behind the reclining-figure mountain
items.note: Pak Meng is a well-known sunset spot, with beachfront restaurants where you can settle in for a while.

items.activity: Have a seafood dinner on Pak Meng beach, then check into a stay around Sikao–Pak Meng to be ready for the morning boat
items.note: Sleeping near the Pak Meng coast makes it easier to reach the pier in time for the early boat the next day.

blocks.title: Where to sleep on the first night
blocks.html: You've got two options for the first night. If you want to wander the town at night, sleep in Trang town and drive out to the pier (about an hour) in the morning. If you'd rather sleep in a bit later and reach the pier quickly, stay around Sikao–Pak Meng, close to the pier. Both work — it comes down to whether you weight the town's food or the ease of the morning more.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Emerald Cave Island Tour, Then Sleep on the Island

blocks.html: This is the heart of the trip. The trick is to not book a one-day round-trip tour, but instead book a tour that drops you on an island to stay over — or take a regular tour boat and tell them to leave you at Koh Kradan or Koh Mook where you've booked your stay. By evening the tour boats are all gone, and the whole beach quiets down to just the handful of people staying the night.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Emerald Cave + Koh Cheuak, then overnight on Koh Kradan / Koh Mook

items.activity: Meet at Pak Meng pier, collect your snorkeling gear, listen to the briefing, and board the tour boat
items.note: Tell the tour when you book that you're staying on the island, so they don't take you back in the evening — and you may get a one-way rate.

items.activity: Reach Koh Mook and swim through the Emerald Cave to the hidden beach inside, where the water glows green
items.note: Wear a life jacket; a guide leads on a rope. The cave is dark at the start, and entry is easier at low tide.

items.activity: Snorkel at Koh Cheuak among the colorful soft coral and schools of fish
items.note: The water's deep with a slight current — hold the rope the guide strings out and you can look around comfortably even if you're not a strong swimmer.

items.activity: Lunch on the boat or at Koh Kradan, a break before the afternoon
items.note: Most tours include lunch, water and fruit. If you're staying over, ask clearly which meals are covered.

items.activity: The boat drops you at Koh Kradan or Koh Mook, wherever you've booked, and you check into your resort
items.note: Koh Kradan has the longest, prettiest white-sand beach, while Koh Mook has a sea-gypsy village and more restaurants.

items.activity: Once the tour boats have gone, swim off the beach, paddle a SUP, or explore the island while it's quiet
items.note: This is when the beach is quietest — the part that makes staying over worth it.

items.activity: Watch the sunset from the beach, then have dinner at your resort or a place on the island
items.note: Restaurants on the island close early, so order dinner on the early side and bring a flashlight, since some spots are dim.

blocks.title: Which to stay on — Koh Kradan or Koh Mook?
blocks.html: Koh Kradan is for people coming purely for a gorgeous beach and clear water — white sand running for a kilometer — but there's almost no village, food and supplies are limited, and stays cost more. Koh Mook has a sea-gypsy village with restaurants and convenience stores, is easier to reach, and has rooms across a range of prices. For a first trip where you want comfort, go with Koh Mook; if you want the most beautiful beach, choose Koh Kradan.

blocks.text: Island Stays — Where Can You Book?

blocks.html: Stays on the Trang islands range from beachfront resorts to simple bungalows. In high season rooms fill very fast, so book at least 2–4 weeks ahead. Here are the real places to stay on the two main islands people overnight on.

items.name: The Sevenseas Resort — Koh Kradan
items.blurb: A beachfront resort on Koh Kradan, inside the national park, fronting the white-sand beach many people call the prettiest in Trang. It offers snorkeling and kayaking, and it's the upmarket pick for anyone who wants to wake up to clear water right in front of them.

items.name: Koh Mook Sivalai Beach Resort — Koh Mook
items.blurb: A resort on a white-sand spit on Koh Mook, with beaches on both sides. The seafront bungalows let you walk straight down to swim, and it's a big photo spot because you can catch both sunrise and sunset from the one island. Mid to upper price.

items.name: Kradan Beach Resort — Koh Kradan
items.blurb: A more affordable stay on Koh Kradan than the big resorts — simple rooms, right on the beach, good for anyone who wants to overnight without paying a premium. There's an on-site restaurant for dinner, handy since options outside are few.

items.name: Reef Resort — Koh Kradan
items.blurb: A quiet, private-feeling resort on Koh Kradan with plenty of space and an outdoor pool — good for couples or anyone after a still, uncrowded stay. It's a touch back from the main beach, the trade-off for the calm.

items.name: Coral Garden Resort — Koh Kradan
items.blurb: A seaside resort on Koh Kradan with both beach and forest behind it, and lots to do — snorkeling, hiking, kayaking. Rooms come as bungalows and singles, making it a fit for groups of friends or families who want more to do than just lie on the beach.
items.meta: Koh Kradan · Lots to do · Mid–upper

items.name: Bungalows in the Koh Mook village
items.blurb: The sea-gypsy village side of Koh Mook has several budget bungalows and guesthouses, within walking distance of restaurants and convenience stores. Good for backpackers or anyone on a budget who wants a simple island overnight — the cheapest starting prices in this group.
items.meta: Koh Mook · In the village · Budget

blocks.title: The honest truth about staying on an island
blocks.html: Staying on an island comes with trade-offs. On some islands the power runs only certain hours or off a generator, the phone signal isn't full everywhere, and the shops close early and charge more than the mainland. The upside is the quietest sea of the day in the morning, and not having to do two boat trips. If you can't go without air-con or internet, read the resort reviews carefully on power and signal before you book.

blocks.text: Day 3 — A Beach Morning, Then the Boat Back

blocks.html: The last day isn't about excitement, but it's the day you get the sea in a version one-day tour groups never see. You wake to a beach that's still quiet, the water calm and clear, and you can swim or sit with a beachfront coffee at your own pace before packing up for the late-morning boat back to shore.

blocks.label: Day 3
blocks.title: Morning on the island + heading home

items.activity: Wake for a morning beach walk while the water is at its stillest, and photograph the empty beach before everyone's up
items.note: First thing in the morning, Koh Kradan's beach is almost empty — the best time for photos.

items.activity: Have breakfast at the resort, then one last swim or SUP off the beach
items.note: Confirm the return boat time with the resort the day before — there are only a few sailings back.

items.activity: Pack up, check out, and take the boat back to shore at Pak Meng or Kuan Tung Ku pier
items.note: The return might be a morning tour boat that swings by, or the resort's own shuttle — ask clearly at check-in.

items.activity: Reach the shore, drive or ride back into Trang town, and stop for a Southern Thai lunch or khanom jeen
items.note: Khanom jeen with Southern curry sauce and fresh veg on the side is a light, well-judged lunch before you move on.

items.activity: Pick up Trang souvenirs — Trang sponge cake, roast pork or local sweets — before the airport or train station
items.note: Trang sponge cake, soft with a hole in the middle, is the classic souvenir, and it boxes up fine to carry on the plane.

blocks.title: Leave a buffer for the return boat
blocks.html: Return boats from the islands are limited and depend on the swell, so don't book your flight or train too tight on the last day. Leave at least 3–4 hours between the boat reaching shore and your onward travel. If the seas are rough the sailing can shift, so a little slack keeps the day from getting stressful.

blocks.text: Roughly What Does This Trip Cost?

blocks.html: The budget depends on the level of island stay you pick and how many of you there are. Here are per-person price ranges based on two people splitting the accommodation and boat. Use them to start planning, but check the exact figures with your stay and tour.

items: Island tour / boat to the island — about ฿850–1,500/person depending on whether it's a big boat or a speedboat. If you're staying over, some operators charge less for one-way.
One night on the island — budget bungalows from about ฿800–1,500/night, beachfront resorts about ฿2,500–6,000+/night; split between two, then averaged per person.
First night in town / Pak Meng — hotels in Trang town about ฿600–1,200/night, resorts around Pak Meng about ฿1,000–2,500/night.
Food for 3 days — roast pork, dim sum, seafood, khanom jeen, roughly ฿600–1,200/person across the whole trip. Trang food is easy on the wallet.
Car / rental — a rental car about ฿1,200–1,500/day, or a motorbike about ฿250–350/day, plus fuel and pier parking at ฿100/day.

blocks.title: How to keep the budget down
blocks.html: If you want to stay on an island cheaply, pick a bungalow in the Koh Mook village over a beachfront resort, and walk Koh Kradan's beach during the tour instead. Book the return with the same tour operator and have them swing by to pick you up — cheaper than chartering a boat twice. As for the food, Trang town is cheap anyway, with plenty of mains under a hundred baht a plate, so there's no need to skimp on that part.

faq.q: Can you really overnight on an island on a 3-day, 2-night Trang trip?
faq.a: Yes. Koh Kradan and Koh Mook both have resorts and bungalows to stay the night. The easiest way is to book a tour that drops you on the island to stay over, or take a regular tour boat and ask them to leave you at the island where you've booked. By evening the tour boats are all gone and the beach quiets down to just the overnight guests. Book your stay ahead in high season, since rooms fill fast.

faq.q: Should I stay on Koh Kradan or Koh Mook?
faq.a: Koh Kradan suits people coming purely for white sand and clear water, but it has few shops and pricier stays. Koh Mook has a sea-gypsy village with restaurants and convenience stores, is easier to reach, and has rooms across a range of prices. For a first trip where you want it easy, go with Koh Mook; if you want the most beautiful beach, choose Koh Kradan.

faq.q: What does a Trang 3-day, 2-night trip like this cost?
faq.a: With two people splitting costs, figure roughly 3,500–7,000 baht per person across the whole trip — about 850–1,500 baht for the boat to the island, one night's island stay averaged per person after splitting two ways, the first night in town, food around 600–1,200 baht, and the car. The figure moves with the level of island stay you pick.

faq.q: When is the best time for this 3-day Trang trip?
faq.a: November to April is best — clear seas, calm water, boats reliably running, and easy island overnights. Avoid the August–September monsoon, when some islands close and the Emerald Cave usually shuts. If you do come then, swap the sea day for a land day instead, such as the Khao Kob sea cave or a waterfall up in the Banthat range.

faq.q: On the first night, should I sleep in Trang town or near the pier?
faq.a: It depends on what you weight. If you want to walk the town and eat at night, sleep in Trang town and drive out to the pier (about an hour) in the morning. If you'd rather sleep in a bit and reach the pier quickly, stay around Sikao–Pak Meng near the pier. Either way you'll make the morning boat if you plan your timing well.
